To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(a) DWV is a causative agent of overt DWV infection in adult honeybees and (b) DWV can be transmitted to pupae and adults by the phoretic mite Varroo destructor.

(1) pupae infected with DWV by injection develop overt DWV infections characterized by deformations of the wings in adult bees; (2) DWV injected into adult bees also causes overt DWV infections; (3) the same DWV dosage injected into adult bees does not result in overt infections; and (4) DWV fed to adult bees results only in covert DWV infections.

(a) pupae injected with a dose of approximately 2500 DWV genome equivalents develop overt infections in adult bees; (b) adult bees injected with a dose greater than 1×107 DWV genome equivalents also develop overt infections; and (c) the transmission of DWV from infected pupae to adult bees is not restricted to a specific age of the pupa.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the horizontal transmission of DWV and the impact of this transmission route on the development of overt infections.
the elucidation of the horizontal transmission of DWV, the causative agent in overt DWV infections.
the elucidation of the pathogenesis of deformed wing syndrome, a severe disease that is caused by the ectoparasite Varroa mite and deformed wing virus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DWV, when transmitted to pupae or adult bees by the ectoparasite Varroa, causes overt DWV infections and deformed wing syndrome in honeybees.
DWV is the cause of overt DWV infection in adult bees, but not the only cause.
the mite transmits DWV horizontally to pupae, and that the resulting overt infections in adult bees depend on the transmission mode and the viral load.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
horizontal transmission of DWV is a complex process and the route of transmission is decisive for the development of overt infections.
the horizontal transmission route of the virus is crucial for the development of overt infections and the deformed-wing symptom.
DWV can be horizontally transmitted from infected pupae to adults, which can result in overt infections, and that the mite is a key player in this process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DWV, when transmitted horizontally to pupae, can cause overt infections.
DWV is the causative factor of the deformed wing syndrome.
the transmission route is a critical factor in the development of deformed wing syndrome.
